implementation_notes: C++20's ranges library turns the chain into composable, lazy adaptors: views::filter and views::transform are the filters, operator| is the pipe, and nothing is materialised between stages because each element is pulled through the whole chain on iteration; ranges::to (C++23) collects a result when a container is needed. This is the default realisation for single-threaded transformations of an existing range, and it replaces hand-written Filter classes entirely. Keep the classic object form for pipelines that are composed at runtime from configuration, or whose stages are asynchronous or long-lived objects with I/O of their own.
pitfalls: Views are non-owning and lazy: a view over a container that goes out of scope, or over a temporary, reads freed memory - keep the source alive for the view's lifetime.
A view is recomputed on every traversal, so reading the same pipeline twice repeats all work (and side effects); materialise with std::ranges::to when multiple passes are needed.
Adaptor order changes cost: filtering before transforming avoids transforming elements that are about to be discarded.

variants.name: Classic Filter objects over stream/queue connectors
variants.implementation_notes: The hand-written POSA structure in C++: an abstract Filter base declares the stage interface (for example apply(std::istream& in, std::ostream& out) or get()/put() over a record type), concrete filters override it, and the pipe is a std::queue or custom std::streambuf that buffers records between stages; a driver owns the vector of filters and pumps source to sink. Virtual dispatch buys runtime composition and reconfiguration that static view adaptor chains cannot express, but it also brings an ownership contract (who deletes stages, who owns buffers) and no laziness or backpressure unless the driver implements them.
pitfalls: The abstract base needs a virtual destructor and the chain must own stages through unique_ptr, otherwise deletion through the base is undefined behaviour.
Hand-rolled std::queue pipes have no bound: one slow filter turns the queue into unbounded memory growth unless a capacity and a blocking policy are added.
Copying a buffer per stage (as above) is convenient but materialises every intermediate; use streambuf-based connectors when streaming matters.
